title: Senior's toolkit: key vaults, KMS and secrets
summary: Read and create keys in Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS, wrap DEKs from .NET, keep Data Protection keys safe and find leaked secrets.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: key vaults, KMS and secrets
steps.body: In production, keys live in a key vault or KMS, apps reach them with a managed identity, and secrets never sit in Git. These are the commands and SDK calls you use to work that way.

toolkit.what: Read a secret from Azure Key Vault. `secret set` writes a new version; old versions stay until you purge them.
flags: only the value, not the whole JSON
plain text, no quotes, for scripts
toolkit.example: az keyvault secret show --vault-name kv-prod --name DbPassword --query value -o tsv

toolkit.what: Create a key-encryption key (KEK) that never leaves the vault. Apps ask the vault to wrap and unwrap with it.
flags: an RSA key held in an HSM (Premium vault)
toolkit.example: az keyvault key create --vault-name kv-prod --name payments-kek --kty RSA-HSM --size 3072 --ops wrapKey unwrapKey

toolkit.what: Envelope encryption from .NET (`Azure.Security.KeyVault.Keys.Cryptography`): wrap a locally generated DEK with the vault's KEK, store the wrapped DEK, unwrap it when you read.
flags: the wrap algorithm for an RSA KEK
the wrapped DEK to store with the data
the exact key version used; store it for rotation
toolkit.when: `DefaultAzureCredential` is fine on a laptop; in production, name the credential you mean

toolkit.what: AWS's envelope encryption in one call: a fresh DEK in plaintext (use it, then wipe it) and the same DEK encrypted under your KMS key (store it).
flags: the KMS key to wrap under
the two Base64 fields in the response

toolkit.what: ASP.NET Core's key ring for cookies, antiforgery tokens and `IDataProtector`. By default keys live on the local disk, which a container loses on redeploy.
flags: instances that share keys must share this name
keep the key ring somewhere every instance can reach
encrypt the key ring at rest with a vault key

toolkit.what: Development secrets stored outside the repository, in your user profile, and read through normal configuration. Not encrypted, not for production.
flags: store a value under a configuration key

toolkit.what: Scan Git history for committed keys, tokens and passwords. Run it in CI and as a pre-commit hook.
flags: hide the secret values in the output
write findings to a file for CI

steps.prompt: After every deploy of the containerised shop, all users are logged out and form posts fail. The log says: `The key {6b2e...} was not found in the key ring.` What is the fix?
options: Persist the Data Protection key ring to shared storage (blob, Redis or a database), set one `SetApplicationName`, and protect it with a vault key
Restart the containers one at a time
steps.explain: Each new container generated a fresh key ring on its own disk, so cookies and antiforgery tokens protected by the old keys cannot be read. Shared, persisted keys survive deploys and work across instances.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of reading one envelope-encrypted record in order.
lines: Load the row: wrapped DEK, KEK version, nonce, ciphertext, tag
Call `UnwrapKeyAsync` with the KEK version stored on the row
Decrypt the ciphertext with `AesGcm` and the unwrapped DEK
Return the plaintext to the caller

steps.prompt: Print only the value of the `DbPassword` secret, as plain text, for a script.
steps.code: az keyvault secret show --vault-name kv-prod --name DbPassword __1__ value __2__ tsv
steps.explain: `--query` takes a JMESPath expression over the JSON result and `-o tsv` prints it without quotes. Both work on every `az` command.

steps.prompt: Match each tool to the situation.
pairs: keep a dev API key out of appsettings.json
read the production DB password in a break-glass shell
get a fresh DEK and its wrapped copy in one call
protect a DEK with a key that never leaves the HSM
find a key someone committed last year

steps.prompt: `gitleaks` finds a live payment API key committed six months ago in a private repository. What do you do first?
options: Rotate (revoke and replace) the key, then check its usage logs; cleaning history comes after
Rewrite Git history to remove it and force-push
Delete the file in a new commit
steps.explain: Assume a secret that was in Git is compromised: clones, forks, CI logs and backups all have it. Rotation is the only step that makes the leaked value useless. History rewriting is clean-up, not a fix.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Before a service ships, ask where each key lives, which identity can use it, and how it rotates. Put `gitleaks` in CI on day one, keep dev secrets in `user-secrets`, and when a secret leaks, rotate first and investigate second.
